text.insert: One durable session owns the project worktree and its head lineage from the baseline sync that opened it until the session closes. Run, PR, and sync are child workflows of the active session; the dispatch lease arbitrates between them and is unchanged by this layer. The session timeline is the ordered truth of how head moved: epoch integrations, remote-application boundaries, PR phases, and save points. Recovery reads the session, not events, to answer where head is and how it got there.

props.title: Decision (2026-08-11) — a durable session container owns head lineage

text.insert: The session is a durable state object above Run, PR, and sync, and it owns head_revision. RunState.head_revision is the mirror that the scheduler plans against.
Between-Run Lineage
ProjectSession resolves the between-runs gap by giving head lineage a durable home that matches the single-active-session rule in the system design:

A sync that arrives during the PR-review week with no active run still records its remote-application boundary in the session timeline; when a run is active, that run additionally references the boundary in its own record.
The session lifecycle ends through the explicit operator action specified in the close decision below.

props.title: Decision (2026-08-11) — sessions close by explicit operator action

text.insert: No automatic transition closes a session; closing is an explicit operator action. The single-active-session rule requires the prior session to close before the next baseline sync opens its successor with a freshly re-anchored worktree.
Close Semantics
Close is valid only when no workflow holds the dispatch lease. If unshipped local work would be orphaned, the action is blocked or requires both confirmation and a named save point.
The absorbed point is the natural moment to close:
Shipped PRs have merged upstream, sync has rebased those PRs in, and the local delta is near zero.
The system neither detects nor enforces that point.
A session left open indefinitely is harmless and keeps accepting workflows.

props.title: Decision (2026-08-12) — head lineage is transactional; save points are evidence anchors

text.insert: The session timeline has two record classes with independent failure policies: head-advancing entries are transactional and commit-creating, while save points are evidence anchors pinned to existing commits. ProjectSession supersedes the system-design notion of one canonical campaign per project; campaign now refers only to PR campaigns.
Lineage and Evidence Failure Policies
epoch_completed and remote_application are the two timeline entry kinds that advance head:
Each entry exists if and only if its commit exists and is written in the same durable step as the integration or sync publish.
If that step fails, the boundary fails loudly rather than logging a warning.
Save points are pure evidence anchors pinned to existing commits:
They never create the commit that carries work.
Their evidence includes reports, the board snapshot, and the headline score.
Boundary hooks and manual creation keep them cheap and frequent.

Because they are evidence anchors rather than commit-creating boundaries, a save-point failure raises both a session blocker and a staleness flag rather than writing a silent log line, a policy motivated by the July 2026 silent boundary-commit failure.
Splitting lineage from evidence has three consequences:
The dashboard's where-we-are contract reads the latest save point, aheadOfBase, and stale from the session.
The intake-and-sessions pages will be re-pointed in a later documentation pass.
The split gives each class the failure policy it needs and gives the system more controllability in the long run.
